back: Administration through the gastrointestinal tract: oral, sublingual, buccal, rectal. Key parameters: convenient but absorption may be slower/variable; oral route undergoes first-pass metabolism; sublingual partly bypasses first pass; rectal absorption is incomplete and partly bypasses portal circulation.

Administration outside the gastrointestinal tract: IV, IM, SC, intradermal, intra-articular and others. Key parameters: useful when rapid effect or unreliable oral absorption matters; IV gives 100% bioavailability; higher risk of infection, tissue injury and dosing errors, because apparently needles needed a side quest.

Most convenient and common route. Advantages: safe, cheap, self-administered. Limits: slow onset, vomiting/food interactions, variable absorption, first-pass metabolism, unsuitable for unconscious patients or drugs destroyed in the gut.

Direct drug delivery into venous blood. Key parameters: fastest onset, 100% bioavailability, precise titration possible; disadvantages include irreversible administration once injected, infection risk, embolism/phlebitis risk and acute toxicity if given too fast.

IM injection usually absorbs faster than SC because muscle is better perfused; depot preparations can prolong action. SC absorption is slower and useful for insulin, heparins and some biologics; avoid irritating substances and poor-perfusion states.

Solutions, suspensions, emulsions, drops, syrups and injections. Key parameters: useful for children or swallowing problems; suspensions must be shaken; dosing accuracy depends on concentration and measuring device.

Ointments, creams, gels, pastes and suppositories. Key parameters: mainly topical/local use, but some rectal/vaginal forms can have systemic effect; vehicle determines absorption, occlusion and skin penetration.

Tablets, capsules, powders, granules and coated/modified-release forms. Key parameters: stable and convenient; modified-release forms should not usually be crushed; enteric coating protects drug or stomach and delays release.

Common dose terms: single dose, daily dose, loading dose, maintenance dose, therapeutic dose, maximal dose, toxic dose and lethal dose. Exam trap: dose depends on indication, route, age, renal/hepatic function and interactions, because biology refuses to be tidy.

Core parts: patient identification, date, drug name, strength, dosage form, quantity, directions for use, route/frequency/duration, prescriber identification and signature. Controlled drugs require stricter formal rules.

Prescription using the international non-proprietary name rather than a brand. Key parameters: supports substitution, reduces cost and avoids brand confusion; some narrow-therapeutic-index or special formulation drugs may need careful non-substitution.

front: Remedy vs medicinal product vs drug substance
back: Drug substance = active pharmacologically effective compound. Medicinal product = finished pharmaceutical product containing active substance plus excipients. Remedy/medicament is the broader therapeutic preparation used to treat, diagnose or prevent disease.

Names include chemical name, generic/INN name and brand/trade name. Key exam idea: INN is preferred for clear communication; brand names differ by country and manufacturer, because naturally medicine needed marketing aliases.

Preclinical testing is followed by clinical phases I-IV. Phase I: safety/dose in healthy volunteers or selected patients. Phase II: efficacy and dose finding. Phase III: large comparative trials. Phase IV: post-marketing pharmacovigilance.

Patient-related factors: age, sex, pregnancy, body weight/composition, genetics, organ function, disease state, receptor sensitivity and circadian rhythm. These modify pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics.

External factors: diet, alcohol, smoking, environmental chemicals, other drugs, adherence, route/formulation and timing. Smoking induces CYP1A2; grapefruit inhibits intestinal CYP3A4; alcohol adds CNS depression and liver risk.

Induction increases enzyme activity and can lower substrate drug levels or increase toxic metabolites. Classic inducers: rifampicin, carbamazepine, phenytoin, phenobarbital, St John's wort and chronic smoking for CYP1A2.

Inhibition decreases metabolism and can raise substrate drug levels. Classic inhibitors: macrolides, azole antifungals, amiodarone, cimetidine, grapefruit juice, ritonavir and some SSRIs. Narrow therapeutic index drugs become dramatic little disasters.

front: Loss of drug effect after long-term use
back: Reduced response can result from tolerance, tachyphylaxis, receptor downregulation, increased metabolism, physiologic compensation or disease progression. Tachyphylaxis is rapid tolerance after repeated doses over short time.

State where drug use becomes compulsive or necessary to avoid withdrawal. Includes psychological craving and physical adaptation. Related concepts: tolerance, withdrawal, reinforcement and addiction behavior.

May be psychological, physical or mixed. Important substances: opioids, alcohol, nicotine, benzodiazepines, stimulants and hallucinogens. Physical dependence means withdrawal occurs when drug is stopped; addiction adds compulsive harmful use.
Options include acamprosate, naltrexone and disulfiram in selected patients. Withdrawal is treated with benzodiazepines plus thiamine before glucose when malnutrition risk exists.
Options: nicotine replacement therapy, varenicline and bupropion. Key parameters: varenicline is a partial nicotinic receptor agonist; bupropion inhibits NE/DA reuptake and lowers craving.

Maintenance/substitution: methadone or buprenorphine. Relapse prevention: naltrexone in selected abstinent patients. Acute overdose: naloxone. Withdrawal is miserable but usually less lethal than alcohol/benzodiazepine withdrawal.

Partial μ-opioid receptor agonist and κ antagonist. Key parameters: used in opioid dependence and pain; ceiling effect for respiratory depression compared with full agonists; can precipitate withdrawal if started too early after full opioid use.

Long-acting opioid receptor antagonist. Key parameters: used for relapse prevention in opioid use disorder after detoxification and for alcohol dependence; contraindicated in current opioid use because it precipitates withdrawal.

Hallucinogens such as LSD/psilocybin mainly act through serotonergic 5-HT2A mechanisms. Intoxication causes perceptual changes, anxiety/panic, sympathetic activation; treatment is calm environment and benzodiazepines if severe agitation.

Increase catecholamine signaling. Examples: methylphenidate, amphetamines, modafinil. Uses include ADHD and narcolepsy; adverse effects: insomnia, appetite loss, hypertension, tachycardia, anxiety and abuse potential.

Psychostimulant; dopamine/noradrenaline reuptake inhibitor. Key parameters: first-line ADHD drug; improves attention and reduces impulsivity; adverse effects include insomnia, appetite suppression, increased BP/HR and tics/anxiety worsening in some patients.

Non-stimulant ADHD drug; selective noradrenaline reuptake inhibitor. Key parameters: useful when stimulants are unsuitable; delayed onset; adverse effects: GI upset, sleep changes, increased BP/HR, rare liver injury or suicidal ideation warning.

Drugs used to improve cognition in specific disorders rather than magically create exam knowledge, tragic as that is. Key examples: acetylcholinesterase inhibitors for Alzheimer disease and memantine as NMDA antagonist.
Central acetylcholinesterase inhibitor for Alzheimer disease. Key parameters: increases cholinergic transmission; adverse effects: nausea, diarrhea, bradycardia, syncope, vivid dreams.
NMDA receptor antagonist used in moderate-to-severe Alzheimer disease. Key parameters: reduces excessive glutamatergic excitotoxicity; adverse effects: dizziness, confusion, headache, constipation.
Muscarinic receptor agonists that mimic acetylcholine directly. Examples: pilocarpine, bethanechol. Effects: miosis, salivation, bronchoconstriction, bradycardia, GI/urinary stimulation.

Direct muscarinic agonist. Key parameters: used in glaucoma and xerostomia; causes miosis and increases secretions; adverse effects reflect cholinergic excess: sweating, salivation, bronchospasm, bradycardia.

Direct muscarinic agonist. Key parameters: stimulates bladder detrusor and GI smooth muscle; used rarely for urinary retention/ileus; adverse effects: diarrhea, bronchospasm, bradycardia, hypotension.

Excess acetylcholine at muscarinic and nicotinic receptors. Findings: salivation, lacrimation, urination, diarrhea, bronchospasm, bradycardia, miosis, fasciculations, weakness. Treatment: atropine plus pralidoxime for organophosphates, airway support.

Antimuscarinic drugs with quaternary ammonium structure; poor CNS penetration. Examples: ipratropium, tiotropium, glycopyrronium, butylscopolamine. Uses: bronchodilation, GI spasm, secretion reduction.
Quaternary antimuscarinic. Key parameters: reduces secretions and causes bronchodilation depending formulation; poor CNS penetration; adverse effects: dry mouth, urinary retention, tachycardia.

Cause vasoconstriction by activating vascular α1 receptors. Examples: phenylephrine, midodrine. Uses: hypotension, nasal decongestion, mydriasis. Adverse effects: hypertension, reflex bradycardia, ischemia.
Selective α1-adrenergic agonist. Key parameters: vasoconstrictor/decongestant/mydriatic; raises BP and may cause reflex bradycardia; little direct β effect.
Prodrug α1 agonist used for symptomatic orthostatic hypotension. Key parameters: increases vascular tone; adverse effects: supine hypertension, piloerection, urinary retention, paresthesias.

Relaxation occurs through reduced intracellular Ca2+, myosin light-chain kinase inhibition, increased cAMP/cGMP or K+ channel opening. Drug examples: β2 agonists increase cAMP; nitrates increase cGMP; calcium blockers reduce Ca2+ entry.

Drugs reducing smooth muscle spasm, especially GI/urogenital. Groups include antimuscarinics such as butylscopolamine and direct smooth muscle relaxants such as drotaverine. Adverse effects depend on mechanism, especially anticholinergic effects.

Drugs that suppress uterine contractions. Examples: β2 agonists, nifedipine, atosiban, magnesium sulfate, indomethacin in selected gestational windows. Risks vary: tachycardia with β2 agonists, hypotension with nifedipine.

Lipid mediators acting on GPCRs. Clinical drugs include misoprostol, dinoprostone, prostacyclin analogues and latanoprost. Effects include gastric protection, uterine contraction/cervical ripening, vasodilation and ocular pressure reduction.

PGE1 analogue. Key parameters: protects gastric mucosa, prevents NSAID ulcers, induces uterine contractions/cervical ripening; adverse effects: diarrhea, cramping; contraindicated in pregnancy unless obstetric use intended.
Prostaglandin F2α analogue for glaucoma. Key parameters: increases uveoscleral outflow and lowers intraocular pressure; adverse effects: iris pigmentation, eyelash growth, conjunctival hyperemia.

Aldosterone-like drugs increase Na+/water retention and K+/H+ excretion in distal nephron. Prototype: fludrocortisone. Uses: adrenal insufficiency, orthostatic hypotension. Toxicity: hypertension, edema, hypokalemia.

Main groups: iron preparations, folic acid, vitamin B12, erythropoiesis-stimulating agents. Choice depends on cause of anemia; throwing iron at every anemia is a classic human ritual but not always clever.

Iron replacement for iron deficiency anemia. Key parameters: ferrous salts; best absorbed on empty stomach with vitamin C but GI intolerance is common; adverse effects: constipation, dark stools, nausea; absorption reduced by antacids/calcium.

Cobalamin replacement for B12 deficiency/pernicious anemia/malabsorption. Key parameters: neurologic deficits may become irreversible; treat B12 deficiency before folate-only correction to avoid masking hematologic signs while nerves continue suffering.

Vitamin B9 replacement; needed for DNA synthesis. Uses: folate deficiency, pregnancy supplementation, methotrexate toxicity support as folinic acid. Deficiency causes megaloblastic anemia without neurologic signs.
Epoetin alfa/darbepoetin stimulate erythropoiesis. Uses: CKD anemia, chemotherapy-associated anemia in selected cases. Risks: hypertension, thrombosis; iron stores must be adequate.

B-complex vitamins and vitamin C. Key parameters: limited storage except B12; deficiency can develop faster; excess usually excreted in urine, though high doses can still cause toxicity or diagnostic confusion, because nothing is allowed to be simple.

Vitamins A, D, E and K. Key parameters: require fat absorption, stored in tissues, higher toxicity risk. Vitamin K is needed for clotting factor activation; vitamin D regulates calcium/phosphate; vitamin A affects vision/epithelium; vitamin E is antioxidant.

Fat-soluble vitamin required for γ-carboxylation of factors II, VII, IX, X and proteins C/S. Uses: deficiency and warfarin reversal support. Deficiency causes bleeding; effect is delayed because new clotting factors must be synthesized.

Important drug groups: vitamin D analogues increase absorption; bisphosphonates/denosumab reduce bone resorption; calcitonin lowers osteoclast activity; cinacalcet activates calcium-sensing receptor and lowers PTH.

Hypokalemia can be caused by loop/thiazide diuretics, β2 agonists and insulin shift; hyperkalemia risk rises with ACEi/ARB/ARNI, aldosterone antagonists, potassium supplements, renal failure and potassium-sparing diuretics.

Iodide is needed for thyroid hormone synthesis. High-dose iodine acutely blocks hormone release and organification (Wolff-Chaikoff effect); radioactive iodine treats hyperthyroidism and thyroid cancer remnants; contrast/amiodarone can disturb thyroid function.

Important drugs include desmopressin, oxytocin, gonadotropins, GnRH analogues, somatostatin analogues and dopamine agonists. They are mostly used as replacement, stimulation, suppression or diagnostic tools.
ADH/V2 receptor analogue. Uses: central diabetes insipidus, nocturnal enuresis, mild hemophilia A/von Willebrand disease. Adverse effect: water retention and hyponatremia.
Posterior pituitary hormone used to induce/augment labor and treat postpartum uterine atony. Adverse effects: uterine hyperstimulation, fetal distress, water intoxication at high doses.

Pulsatile GnRH stimulates gonadotropins; continuous GnRH agonists suppress LH/FSH after flare. Uses: prostate cancer, endometriosis, precocious puberty, assisted reproduction. Antagonists suppress immediately.

Block androgen effects or synthesis. Examples: spironolactone, cyproterone, flutamide/bicalutamide/enzalutamide, finasteride/dutasteride. Uses: prostate cancer, hirsutism, BPH depending drug. Adverse effects: sexual dysfunction, gynecomastia, liver toxicity for some.

Synthetic androgenic/anabolic drugs. Medical uses are limited; misuse causes acne, infertility, testicular atrophy, virilization, liver injury, dyslipidemia, hypertension and psychiatric effects. Tiny price for gym mythology, apparently.

Agents enhancing immune responses. Examples include vaccines, interferons, colony-stimulating factors and some adjuvant-like therapies. Uses: infection prevention, immunodeficiency support, selected cancers; toxicity often reflects immune activation.

Filgrastim/pegfilgrastim stimulate neutrophil production via G-CSF receptor. Uses: chemotherapy-induced neutropenia and stem cell mobilization. Adverse effects: bone pain, leukocytosis, splenic rupture rarely.

Core treatment uses DMARDs: methotrexate first-line unless contraindicated; alternatives/add-ons include sulfasalazine, hydroxychloroquine, leflunomide, biologics such as anti-TNF drugs and JAK inhibitors. NSAIDs/steroids help symptoms but do not replace DMARDs.
DMARD and antimalarial. Uses: rheumatoid arthritis, lupus, malaria in selected settings. Key adverse effect: retinal toxicity, so eye monitoring matters; also GI upset and QT risk.

DMARD inhibiting dihydroorotate dehydrogenase and pyrimidine synthesis. Uses: rheumatoid arthritis. Adverse effects: hepatotoxicity, hypertension, diarrhea, teratogenicity; cholestyramine washout can accelerate elimination.

Targeted synthetic DMARDs inhibiting Janus kinase signaling. Examples: tofacitinib, baricitinib, upadacitinib. Risks: serious infections, herpes zoster, thrombosis, lipid changes and lab abnormalities.

Immune-mediated adverse drug reaction. Can be IgE-mediated immediate allergy with urticaria/anaphylaxis or delayed T-cell mediated rash/severe cutaneous reactions. Management: stop culprit, treat reaction, document clearly; avoid rechallenge when serious.

First-line treatment is intramuscular adrenaline. Also: airway/oxygen, IV fluids, remove trigger, antihistamines and corticosteroids as adjuncts, bronchodilators for bronchospasm. Do not delay adrenaline while decorating the patient with secondary drugs.

May be predictable dose-related toxicity or idiosyncratic. Patterns: hepatocellular, cholestatic, mixed. Important drugs: paracetamol, isoniazid, valproate, methotrexate, amiodarone, azoles, statins. Monitor symptoms and liver enzymes where appropriate.

Mechanisms include hemodynamic injury, tubular toxicity, interstitial nephritis and crystal nephropathy. Examples: NSAIDs, ACEi/ARB in susceptible patients, aminoglycosides, vancomycin, amphotericin B, cisplatin, acyclovir crystals.

Important patterns: bleeding with anticoagulants/antiplatelets, agranulocytosis with clozapine/thionamides, aplastic anemia rarely, thrombocytopenia with heparin, hemolysis in G6PD deficiency with oxidant drugs.

front: Drug adverse effects on cardiovascular system
back: Key toxicities: QT prolongation/torsades, bradycardia/AV block, hypotension, hypertension, edema, heart failure worsening and cardiomyopathy. Examples: anthracyclines cause cardiomyopathy; non-DHP CCBs cause AV block; NSAIDs can worsen BP/HF.

front: Management of allergic diseases except asthma
back: Main drugs: second-generation H1 antihistamines for rhinitis/urticaria, intranasal corticosteroids for allergic rhinitis, topical steroids for dermatitis, mast cell stabilizers in selected cases, adrenaline for anaphylaxis.

Prevent mast cell degranulation and mediator release. Examples: cromolyn, nedocromil, ketotifen. Mainly prophylactic in allergic rhinitis/conjunctivitis/asthma; not useful for acute anaphylaxis or acute bronchospasm.

Major groups: 5-HT3 antagonists, D2 antagonists, H1 antihistamines, antimuscarinics, NK1 antagonists, cannabinoids and corticosteroids. Choice depends on cause: motion sickness, chemotherapy, postoperative nausea, vestibular disease or migraine.

Aprepitant/fosaprepitant block substance P NK1 receptors. Key parameters: used especially for chemotherapy-induced nausea/vomiting; often combined with 5-HT3 antagonist and dexamethasone; CYP interactions matter.

Methanol is metabolized to formic acid causing metabolic acidosis and visual toxicity. Treatment: fomepizole or ethanol, bicarbonate for severe acidosis, folinic/folic acid, hemodialysis in severe poisoning.

Acute intoxication: supportive care, glucose only after thiamine if malnourished. Withdrawal: benzodiazepines are first-line; severe withdrawal may cause seizures/delirium tremens. Correct fluids, electrolytes and vitamins.

General poisoning tools: remove from exposure, skin/eye decontamination, activated charcoal for selected recent oral ingestions, gastric lavage rarely, whole bowel irrigation for selected sustained-release/iron/body packer cases.

Options: urinary alkalinization for selected weak acids such as salicylates, multiple-dose activated charcoal for some drugs, hemodialysis for methanol, ethylene glycol, lithium, salicylates and severe renal-clearable toxins.

Naloxone-opioids; flumazenil-benzodiazepines; N-acetylcysteine-paracetamol; atropine/pralidoxime-organophosphates; fomepizole-methanol/ethylene glycol; hydroxocobalamin-cyanide; methylene blue-methemoglobinemia; protamine-heparin; vitamin K/PCC-warfarin.

Main antiviral targets: viral entry/uncoating, polymerases, reverse transcriptase, integrase, protease, neuraminidase and immune modulation. Because viruses use host cells, selectivity is harder than with bacteria, naturally making life worse.

Acyclovir resistance usually involves viral thymidine kinase deficiency or altered DNA polymerase. Alternative for resistant severe HSV/VZV: foscarnet, which does not require activation by viral thymidine kinase but is nephrotoxic.
Neuraminidase inhibitors: oseltamivir, zanamivir, peramivir. Best when started early. Baloxavir inhibits cap-dependent endonuclease. Adamantanes are largely obsolete because of resistance.

Important drugs: tenofovir and entecavir suppress HBV polymerase/reverse transcription. They reduce viral replication but usually do not eradicate covalently closed circular DNA, hence chronic management exists to annoy everyone.

Direct-acting antivirals target NS3/4A protease, NS5A or NS5B polymerase. Examples: sofosbuvir, ledipasvir, velpatasvir, glecaprevir/pibrentasvir. Modern combinations achieve high cure rates when taken correctly.

Choose based on likely pathogen, infection site, severity, host factors, local resistance and culture results. Use correct dose/duration, de-escalate when possible, and remember source control. Antibiotics are not decorative confetti.

Drug penetration differs by tissue. CNS penetration matters in meningitis; intracellular penetration for atypicals; urinary concentration for UTIs; bone/prostate/biofilm penetration can be difficult. Inflammation may increase barrier permeability.

Common exam toxicities: β-lactam allergy, macrolide QT/CYP interactions, aminoglycoside nephro/ototoxicity, tetracycline teeth/photosensitivity, fluoroquinolone tendons/QT/CNS, clindamycin C. difficile, vancomycin nephrotoxicity/red man syndrome.
Key groups: fluoroquinolones inhibit DNA gyrase/topoisomerase; rifampicin inhibits bacterial RNA polymerase; metronidazole damages DNA in anaerobes; nitrofurantoin damages bacterial DNA in urine.
Natural penicillins: penicillin G and V. Best for susceptible Gram-positive cocci, anaerobes above diaphragm and spirochetes. Destroyed by β-lactamases; main adverse effect is hypersensitivity.

Aminopenicillins and antipseudomonal penicillins expand Gram-negative coverage. Examples: amoxicillin/ampicillin and piperacillin. Often combined with β-lactamase inhibitors such as clavulanate, sulbactam or tazobactam.
Include polymyxins such as colistin and bacitracin. Polymyxins disrupt Gram-negative bacterial membranes and are reserved for resistant infections; major toxicity: nephrotoxicity and neurotoxicity.

front: Targeted anticancer therapy - nucleic acid repair/epigenetics
back: Examples: PARP inhibitors impair DNA repair in BRCA-mutated tumors; HDAC inhibitors and DNA methyltransferase inhibitors modify gene expression. Toxicities often include myelosuppression, GI effects and fatigue depending drug.

Olaparib and related drugs block poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase DNA repair. Key parameters: useful in BRCA/HRD-associated cancers; adverse effects: anemia, fatigue, nausea, myelosuppression; rare MDS/AML risk.

Bortezomib/carfilzomib inhibit proteasomal protein degradation. Uses: multiple myeloma and some lymphomas. Adverse effects: peripheral neuropathy especially bortezomib, thrombocytopenia, herpes zoster reactivation.
Targeted drugs can promote cancer cell apoptosis by blocking survival proteins. Example: venetoclax inhibits BCL-2 and is used in selected leukemias/lymphomas. Key risk: tumor lysis syndrome.

Cancer vaccines aim to generate antitumor immune response; adoptive therapies such as CAR-T cells transfer engineered immune cells. Toxicities include cytokine release syndrome and neurotoxicity for CAR-T therapy.

front: Mechanisms of resistance to cytostatic therapy
back: Resistance mechanisms: increased drug efflux via P-glycoprotein, altered targets, enhanced DNA repair, failure of apoptosis, drug inactivation, reduced activation of prodrugs and poor tumor penetration.

Common toxicities reflect damage to rapidly dividing cells: myelosuppression, mucositis, alopecia, infertility, nausea/vomiting. Specific toxicities: anthracycline cardiomyopathy, cisplatin nephro/ototoxicity, cyclophosphamide cystitis, bleomycin pulmonary fibrosis.

Children differ in absorption, body water/fat, protein binding, hepatic metabolism, renal elimination and receptor sensitivity. Doses often use weight/body surface area; avoid tetracyclines in young children and aspirin in viral illness.

Older adults have reduced renal clearance, altered body composition, polypharmacy and higher sensitivity to CNS, anticholinergic and hypotensive drugs. Start low, titrate carefully, review medication lists, and deprescribe the nonsense.
